overlap.title: Who prompted David's census?
overlap.summary: Samuel attributes the prompting to the LORD's anger; Chronicles names Satan.
overlap.reasoning: The passages explicitly assign the prompting to different agents. A theological explanation can posit divine permission and an intermediate agent, but neither verse states that combined explanation.
overlap.scope: A difference in narrated causation; it does not independently establish a supernatural cause.

overlap.title: Who were the “sons of God” who took the daughters of men?
overlap.summary: Genesis 6 says the sons of God took wives from the daughters of men and that children were born to them, just before the Lord resolves to destroy man. The passage does not say who the sons of God were.
overlap.reasoning: The passage sets two groups beside each other, the sons of God and the daughters of men, and tells of their marriages and children immediately before God sees that the wickedness of man is great. Nothing earlier in Genesis uses the phrase “sons of God”, and the passage does not explain it. Verse 4 also leaves open how the giants are related to these unions: it says they were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men, without saying that the giants were the children. In the Hebrew edition quoted, the two words for “sons of God” in Genesis 6:2 are the same two words as in Job 1:6, where the sons of God present themselves before the Lord. Brenton’s Greek has “sons of God” in Genesis 6 and “angels of God” in Job 1:6.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have identified the sons of God as heavenly beings, as men of one family line marrying women of another, or as rulers. Each is an interpretation; the passage states none of them, and this record asserts none. The same Hebrew words in Job show that the phrase is shared; shared wording does not settle what it means in Genesis 6. Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels that sinned, and are read by some as referring to this passage; neither mentions Genesis 6, marriage or daughters of men. Matthew 22:30 is cited by others against the first reading; it speaks of the resurrection and of angels in heaven and does not mention Genesis 6 either. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “sons of God” (11 verses: Genesis 6:2, 6:4; Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; John 1:12; Romans 8:14, 8:19; Philippians 2:15; 1 John 3:1, 3:2) and all were read; Matthew 22:30, Jude 1:6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4–5 were read as well. None says who the sons of God of Genesis 6 were. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G tag is proposed: in Genesis 6:2 and 6:4 Brenton’s Greek agrees with the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: “again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel” — for what, before David numbered the people?
overlap.summary: The chapter opens with the Lord’s anger already kindled “against Israel”, before describing David being moved to number the people. Seventy thousand die. David says the sin is his and asks of the people, “these sheep, what have they done?” The verses compared name no act of Israel that the anger was for, and do not say to what earlier anger “again” looks back.
overlap.reasoning: In the order of 24:1 the anger comes first and the numbering second: the anger is “against Israel”, and David is moved “against them”. In that presentation, the numbering is not identified as the cause of the opening anger; the sentence’s order alone does not establish an independently dated sequence. The sin the chapter does name is David’s (“I have sinned greatly in that I have done”), and David himself separates the people from it (“these sheep, what have they done?”), yet it is the people who die. “Again” says that this anger follows an earlier one, and the verse does not name it. The parallel at 1 Chronicles 21:1 opens without any statement of anger, and 1 Chronicles 21:7 places God’s displeasure after the numbering, “with this thing”. So the verses compared leave unstated what Israel had done, and the answer bears on how the deaths of 24:15 are to be understood.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that “again” looks back to the famine of 21:1, which that verse lays to Saul and his house; that the anger was for Israel’s part in the revolts told earlier in the book; that the people shared in some fault of the numbering itself; that the cause is simply not given. Limits: 24:1 states that the anger was against Israel and does not say it was without cause; David’s question at 24:17 is his own speech and is not a statement by the narrator that the people were innocent; Joab’s words at 1 Chronicles 21:3 speak of “a cause of trespass to Israel” that the numbering would bring, which concerns the numbering and not the earlier anger; the only other verse of 2 Samuel found with the phrase is 6:7, where the anger is against Uzzah, a single man. This record does not take up who moved David, on which 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 are the subject of a separate record; the two verses are quoted here only for what they say of the anger. Check made: 2 Samuel 24:1–25 and 1 Chronicles 21:1–8 were read in the KJV, 2 Samuel 24:1, 24:3, 24:10, 24:15 and 24:17 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, 21:3 and 21:7 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “anger of the Lord was kindled” in 2 Samuel finds 6:7 and 24:1. That is a word search and a reading of the verses named, not a reading of the whole book. These checked verses do not say for what the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. overlap.title: Uz, Hul and Gether: sons of Shem, or sons of Aram?
overlap.summary: Chronicles lists Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech in one run under “The sons of Shem”. Genesis gives Shem five sons and calls Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash “the children of Aram”. Brenton’s Greek of the Chronicles verse names only the first two sons of Shem and none of the four.
overlap.reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew of Chronicles nothing separates Aram from the four names that follow: all nine stand under “The sons of Shem”. Genesis ends Shem’s sons at Aram and gives the four to Aram. Brenton’s Greek of the Chronicles verse stops after the second name, so this verse has neither the four names nor Arphaxad, Lud and Aram; the next verse printed, 24, begins with Arphaxad.
overlap.scope: G applies at 1 Chronicles 1:17, where the Greek verse is much shorter than the KJV. Genesis 10:22–23 is context. The two KJV statements can stand together if “sons” in Chronicles takes in grandsons, or if the Chronicles list is a shortened copy of Genesis that leaves out the words “and the children of Aram”; the verse does not say either. The record does not claim that Meshech and Mash are the same person or different persons. It does not say why the Greek is shorter. No H is proposed: the KJV follows the Hebrew in both books. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined.
